chapters.situation: Gandhi is now an advocate of the Natal Supreme Court with merchant retainers, and leads the fight against the Franchise Bill.
chapters.summary: Gandhi founds the Natal Indian Congress on 22 May 1894, keeping the name 'Congress' despite its unpopularity with British Conservatives. He is secretary, chases subscriptions, and once sits up all night at Tongaat until a host pays his promised £6. He keeps strict receipts, never borrows, teaches members to run meetings, starts an association for colonial-born Indians, and writes two pamphlets on Natal's Indians.

updates.gandhi: Founder and secretary of the Natal Indian Congress. Pays £1 a month himself and keeps every penny accounted for.
updates.abdulla: Heads the Congress subscription list at £2 a month; the founding meeting is held in his room.
updates.nic: Founded 22 May 1894. Subscriptions become annual (£3 minimum). It never goes into debt, and has a colonial-born educational association and a propaganda arm.
updates.publicwork: Gandhi's rules: never run public work on borrowed money, issue receipts for everything, print nothing until funds allow, keep accounts strictly.
updates.simplicity: Even the Congress runs lean: a cyclostyle machine instead of printed receipt books.
updates.indians_sa: Colonial-born educated Indians are drawn in through their own association.
updates.truth: 'Without properly kept accounts it is impossible to maintain truth in its pristine purity.'

chapters.situation: The new Natal Indian Congress serves merchants, clerks and colonial-born youths, but not yet the poorest indentured labourers.
chapters.summary: Balasundaram, a Tamil indentured labourer, arrives at Gandhi's office bleeding, with two teeth knocked out by his master, holding his headgear in his hand as required before Europeans. Gandhi gets a medical certificate and a summons. Rather than seek punishment, he arranges for the indenture to be transferred to a kinder European employer. Word spreads among labourers as far as Madras, and they begin streaming to Gandhi as their friend.

updates.gandhi: Takes up Balasundaram's case and becomes known as the friend of indentured labourers. Asks Balasundaram to put his scarf back on.
updates.balasundaram: Beaten by his European master; Gandhi gets his indenture transferred to a new employer. His case becomes famous among labourers in Natal and Madras.
updates.indenture: An indentured labourer who leaves his master can be jailed. Sir William Hunter called the system almost as bad as slavery.
updates.tamil: Tamil labourers begin to see Gandhi as their advocate.
updates.racism: Indians are expected to remove their headgear before any European.
updates.compromise: Gandhi seeks the man's release, not his employer's punishment.

chapters.situation: Since Balasundaram's case, indentured labourers have been coming to Gandhi with their troubles.
chapters.summary: In 1894 Natal proposes a £25 annual tax on ex-indentured Indians who stay on rather than return or re-indenture. White settlers had welcomed Indian labour but now resent free Indians as farmers and traders. The Congress campaigns hard, and Viceroy Lord Elgin approves a reduced £3 tax, which Gandhi calls a breach of trust. A family of four could owe £12 a year on 14 shillings a month. It will take twenty years and a mass struggle to abolish it.

updates.gandhi: Leads the Congress campaign against the indenture tax and calls the Viceroy's consent a betrayal of India's trust.
updates.elgin: Rejects the £25 tax but approves a £3 poll tax, which Gandhi calls a serious blunder.
updates.gokhale: Mentioned ahead of time: a broken promise to him will spark the final campaign against the tax two decades later.
updates.nic: Campaigns against the tax; may have helped cut it from £25 to £3.
updates.indenture: The £3 tax falls on every freed labourer and on wives, sons over 16 and daughters over 13. It is not abolished until 1914, after a mass struggle.
updates.indians_sa: White hostility grows as freed Indians prosper as gardeners, landowners and traders.

chapters.situation: Gandhi is absorbed in public service in Natal, which he now sees as his road to God.
chapters.summary: Gandhi befriends Spencer Walton of the South Africa General Mission, who never presses him to convert. Guided by Raychandbhai, he reads the Upanishads, Max Müller, books on Muhammad and Zoroaster, and Tolstoy, and comes to appreciate Hinduism more. He finds Wesleyan sermons dull. A Christian family asks him to stop visiting after their small son, inspired by Gandhi, starts refusing meat.

updates.gandhi: Serves the community as his path to self-realization. Reads widely in Hinduism, Islam and Tolstoy and tries some yogic practices.
updates.walton: Head of the South Africa General Mission. He and Mrs. Walton become close friends who live their faith openly without proselytizing.
updates.tolstoy: 'The Gospels in Brief' and 'What to Do?' deepen Gandhi's sense of the 'infinite possibilities of universal love'.
updates.religion: Gandhi's regard for Hinduism grows without prejudice against other faiths. He has made 'the religion of service' his own.
updates.islam: Washington Irving and Carlyle raise the Prophet in Gandhi's estimation.
updates.christianity: Gandhi finds the Wesleyan church uninspiring and compares Jesus unfavourably with Buddha's compassion for all creatures.
updates.diet: A child's turn to fruit costs Gandhi a family's friendship. He concludes that what he eats influences others more than what he says.

chapters.situation: Gandhi has set up a household in Durban suited to his position as the community's barrister.
chapters.summary: Gandhi's household includes a clever companion, a cook and boarding clerks. The companion makes Gandhi suspect an innocent clerk, who leaves. A temporary cook leads Gandhi home to find a prostitute in the companion's room. Gandhi throws the man out by threatening to call the police. He sees it as a repeat of his old mistake of trying to reform a bad friend, and regrets never fully making amends to the wronged clerk.

updates.gandhi: Expels a deceitful housemate and regrets wrongly suspecting his clerk. Begins a life of greater detachment.
updates.companion: Poisons Gandhi against a clerk and brings a prostitute into the house. Gandhi throws him out.
updates.mehtab: The pattern repeats: as with the schoolboy friend, Gandhi trusted a bad character he hoped to reform.
updates.ahimsa: 'A rift is a rift': Gandhi cannot fully repair the injustice done to his clerk.
updates.simplicity: A household kept up for prestige brings trouble.

chapters.situation: After three years in South Africa Gandhi has a good practice and is indispensable to the community.
chapters.summary: In mid-1896 Gandhi sails home for six months to fetch his family and rouse Indian opinion, leaving Adamji Miyakhan as Congress secretary. On the S.S. Pongola he studies Tamil and Urdu, to be closer to the Tamil labourers and the Muslims. He argues with the captain, a Plymouth Brother, and becomes surer that religion and morality are one. He lands at Calcutta.

updates.gandhi: Sails to India in mid-1896 to bring his family back to Natal. Studies Tamil and Urdu on board.
updates.adamji: Appointed secretary of the Natal Indian Congress in Gandhi's absence, and proves an excellent one.
updates.tamil: Gandhi studies Tamil to repay the 'faith, perseverance and selfless sacrifice' of the Dravidian labourers.
updates.religion: Gandhi is confirmed in his view that religion and morality are synonymous.
updates.indenture: Gandhi calls the £3 tax 'an open sore'.

chapters.situation: Back in India on a six-month visit, Gandhi plans to rouse Indian opinion about South Africa's Indians.
chapters.summary: After missing his train at Allahabad, Gandhi meets the editor of The Pioneer, a meeting he later says led to his being lynched in Natal. In Rajkot he writes the 'Green Pamphlet', posted by neighbourhood children for used stamps. Reuters cables an exaggerated summary of it to Natal. When plague threatens, he inspects latrines: the rich are filthiest, while the untouchables' homes, which he visits for the first time, are spotless.

updates.gandhi: Publishes the Green Pamphlet and volunteers on Rajkot's plague committee. Visits untouchables' quarters for the first time.
updates.chesney: Gives Gandhi a fair hearing and is the first to comment on the Green Pamphlet. The interview sets off the events leading to the Natal lynching.
updates.greenpamphlet: 10,000 copies sent across India. Reuters' three-line exaggerated summary reaches Natal with consequences to come.
updates.sanitation: On the Rajkot plague committee: the latrines of the rich are filthiest, and even the Vaishnava temple is dirty.
updates.untouchability: Gandhi's first visit to untouchables' quarters finds them cleaner than upper-class homes.
updates.publicwork: Gandhi uses child volunteers for the first time; two of them later become his coworkers.

chapters.situation: Gandhi is in Rajkot campaigning about South Africa through the Green Pamphlet and serving on the plague committee.
chapters.summary: Gandhi explains his sincere loyalty to the British Empire, shown in joining Rajkot's Jubilee committee and teaching the National Anthem, though he later objects to its line about scattering enemies. He meets Justices Ranade and Tyabji and the 'Lion of Bombay', Pherozeshah Mehta, who promises a public meeting. He nurses his dying brother-in-law at home, and nursing becomes a passion.

updates.gandhi: A sincerely loyal subject of the Empire at this stage. Nurses his brother-in-law until his death and finds that nursing has become a passion.
updates.pherozeshah: Receives Gandhi 'as a loving father' and arranges a public meeting in Bombay.
updates.ranade: Advises Gandhi to see Pherozeshah Mehta.
updates.tyabji: Sympathetic, but sends Gandhi to Pherozeshah Mehta.
updates.booth: Later agrees with Gandhi that the anthem's lines about 'knavish tricks' don't fit ahimsa, and writes a new anthem.
updates.loyalty: Gandhi believes British rule is beneficial and that colour prejudice is un-British and temporary. The anthem's call to scatter enemies later jars him.
updates.nursing: Becomes a passion, but 'service which is rendered without joy helps neither the servant nor the served.'
updates.ahimsa: Gandhi later objects to the anthem asking God to frustrate 'knavish tricks'.

chapters.situation: Pherozeshah Mehta has agreed to hold a public meeting in Bombay on South African Indians, the day after Gandhi's brother-in-law dies.
chapters.summary: Pherozeshah insists Gandhi write and print his speech overnight. At the packed meeting Gandhi's voice fails, the audience calls for Wacha, and Wacha reads the speech to great effect. Several men promise to come to South Africa but none do. His old friend Pestonji Padshah urges him to stay and serve India, which only makes him firmer in his resolve.

updates.gandhi: Exhausted after nursing, he cannot be heard at the Bombay meeting. Wacha reads his speech, and Gandhi becomes firmer in his commitment to South Africa.
updates.pherozeshah: Insists on a printed speech and cheers Gandhi on at the meeting.
updates.wacha: Reads Gandhi's speech to a quiet, applauding audience.
updates.deshpande: Tries to read the speech for Gandhi; promises to go to South Africa but never does.
updates.padshah: Refuses to help and advises Gandhi to stay in India: 'Let us win self-government here.'
updates.rustomji: Mentioned as having made up for a Parsi friend's broken promise to join the cause.
updates.gita: Gandhi cites the Gita on doing one's own duty even if one fails.
updates.shyness: Still unable to make himself heard by a big audience.

chapters.situation: Encouraged by the Bombay meeting, Gandhi tours other Indian cities to win support for South Africa's Indians.
chapters.summary: In Poona, Tilak advises a non-party chairman and sends Gandhi to the scholar Bhandarkar, who agrees to preside. Gandhi meets Gokhale for the first time and feels instantly at home: Pherozeshah is like the Himalaya, Tilak the ocean, but Gokhale the Ganges. In Madras the Balasundaram story moves a crowded meeting, the Green Pamphlet sells out, and the editor G. Parameshvaran Pillay opens his paper to Gandhi.

updates.gandhi: Wins support from both camps in Poona and an enthusiastic welcome in Madras. Meets the man who will become his political guru.
updates.tilak: Generously advises a non-party chairman and offers all help. Gandhi sees the secret of his popularity.
updates.gokhale: First meeting at Fergusson College. He examines Gandhi like a schoolmaster and wins his heart. His place in Gandhi's political life is 'absolutely unique'.
updates.bhandarkar: Breaks his rule of staying out of politics to preside over the Poona meeting.
updates.pillay: Puts The Madras Standard at Gandhi's disposal.
updates.balasundaram: His case moves the Madras audience deeply.
updates.greenpamphlet: A second edition of 10,000 copies sells fast in Madras.
updates.madras: An enthusiastic meeting at Pachaiappa Hall.
updates.poona: Joint meeting of both political camps, with Bhandarkar presiding.

chapters.situation: After successes in Bombay, Poona and Madras, Gandhi travels to Calcutta, where he knows no one.
chapters.summary: Calcutta is hard going: a Bengal Club bars Indians from its drawing room, Surendranath Banerji is doubtful, the Maharajas are cold, and an editor sends Gandhi away. But Saunders of The Englishman befriends him, impressed by his fairness even to the white side. Before he can hold a meeting a cable arrives: 'Parliament opens January. Return soon.' In December Gandhi sails on Dada Abdulla's Courland with Kasturbai, two sons and his widowed sister's son, alongside the Naderi with about 800 passengers.

updates.gandhi: Recalled to Natal by cable. Sails in December 1896 with his family on the Courland.
updates.surendranath: Doubts Calcutta will take interest; sends Gandhi to the Maharajas.
updates.saunders: Cross-examines Gandhi, then becomes a friend and ally, valuing his 'freedom from exaggeration'.
updates.abdulla: His firm has bought the Courland; he carries Gandhi's family free.
updates.kasturba: Sails to South Africa with Gandhi for the first time.
updates.harilal: Sails to South Africa with his parents.
updates.manilal: Sails to South Africa with his parents.
updates.gokuldas: Joins the family on the voyage to South Africa.
updates.calcutta: A cold reception, except from The Englishman and The Statesman.
updates.courland: Sails in December 1896 alongside the Naderi with about 800 Indian passengers, half bound for the Transvaal.
updates.truth: 'We win justice quickest by rendering justice to the other party.'

status.gandhi: Sailing back to Natal with family, Dec 1896
status.kasturba: On her way to South Africa

chapters.situation: Gandhi is sailing back to Natal for the first time with his wife and children, recalled urgently for the coming legislative session.
chapters.summary: Gandhi dresses his family in the Parsi style, with shoes, stockings, knives and forks, which they accept only out of obedience. Four days from Natal a 24-hour gale makes Muslims, Hindus and Christians pray together, and they forget God once it passes. Gandhi, a good sailor, moves among the frightened passengers and makes friends. The ships anchor at Durban on 18 or 19 December, but 'the real storm was still to come'.

updates.gandhi: Imposes European and Parsi dress on his family. Comforts passengers through the gale.
updates.kasturba: Made to wear a Parsi sari, shoes and stockings and to use knives and forks, out of obedience rather than conviction.
updates.harilal: Dressed in Parsi coat and trousers for the new country.
updates.manilal: Dressed in Parsi coat and trousers for the new country.
updates.dress: Gandhi still believes Indians must look 'civilized' by European standards to have influence. He later says they all felt freer after casting it off.
updates.courland: A violent gale four days out unites the passengers in prayer. They anchor at Durban on 18 or 19 December 1896.
updates.religion: In danger, all faiths turn to the one God; when the danger passes, so does their prayer.
